content_voiceover: This smear is the single most important morphology image for TMA on the boards, and you need to be able to spot these findings instantly. The arrows point to schistocytes, fragmented red blood cells that form when RBCs are sheared apart passing through vessels partially occluded by platelet rich microthrombi, and helmet cells, a specific schistocyte shape with a crescent, helmet like outline. These fragments are the morphologic signature of mechanical intravascular hemolysis, and finding more than about one percent schistocytes on a smear in the right clinical context is essentially required to diagnose MAHA. You'll also see polychromasia, larger bluish gray red cells reflecting a robust reticulocyte response to the ongoing hemolysis, and occasional nucleated RBCs, which signal marrow stress from severe hemolysis pushing out immature erythroid precursors early. Finally notice the striking absence of platelets on this field, consistent with the severe consumptive thrombocytopenia of TTP or other TMAs, since platelets are being consumed to form the microvascular thrombi. On an exam, if you're shown a smear like this with fragments and no platelets, your differential should immediately jump to TMA, and specifically TTP if severe thrombocytopenia and neurologic findings are present without another clear cause.
keypoints: Schistocytes and helmet cells = mechanical hemolysis signature
Polychromasia = brisk reticulocyte response to hemolysis
Absent/scant platelets on smear = consumptive thrombocytopenia
keypoint_voiceover: On boards, recognize schistocytes and helmet cells instantly as the morphologic fingerprint of microangiopathic hemolysis, RBCs sheared apart by microvascular thrombi. Polychromasia shows the marrow is responding with reticulocytes, and nucleated red cells signal marrow stress. The scarcity of platelets on the field reflects consumptive thrombocytopenia, and together these findings should trigger a TMA workup.
